home.title: Your NIS 2 implementation
home.lead: One item after the other. What you set aside waits for you on the right.

intro.eyebrow: NIS 2 for companies with 50 to 150 employees
intro.title: You are in the right place.
intro.lead: You have been asked to take care of NIS 2 and do not know where to start? That is how almost everyone feels. We go through it with you, item by item.

points.title: One thing at a time
points.text: You only ever see one item. We explain it before you enter anything.

points.title: Methods we recommend
points.text: Where a proven method exists, we show it to you. You decide whether to adopt it.

points.title: Leaving things open is fine
points.text: What cannot be done yet, you set aside and carry on with the next item.

intro.firstItems: The first items on your path

waitReasons.letter: I'm waiting for a letter, for example an activation letter for the portal
waitReasons.ask: I need to ask someone first
waitReasons.decide: We have to decide this internally

1_1.headline: Get management trained
missed: The training should cover the goals of § 38(3) BSIG: recognising and assessing risks and risk management, and judging what they mean for your company's services.

The law says "regularly" and names neither an interval nor a duration. The BSI recommends a thorough first training followed by refresher trainings, with duration and interval set by your risk exposure.

learn.title: Training for management
body: Whoever runs the company takes part in information security training regularly. This applies to every member of management personally.
We offer a course for this on this platform. You can also choose any other provider; the law does not require providers to be accredited.
learn.duty: Management has to take part in training regularly. How often and for how long, the law does not say.
learn.link: Go to the course for management

record.title: What records can look like
record.caption: One line per person and training:

rows.name: Anna Example, managing director
rows.detail: In-person training at a training institute, 12 March 2026, certificate of attendance

rows.name: Jonas Sample, managing director
rows.detail: Online course, 3 April 2026, certificate as a PDF

rows.name: Lea Specimen, managing director
rows.detail: Webinar by an industry association, 20 May 2026, screenshot of attendance

record.note: The law prescribes no format. In-person training, an online course, a webinar or an in-house session all come into question. Record who took part, when, and what it covered.

trainings.title: One line per person
trainings.lead: Enter the latest training for every member of management. You can attach proof; after a webinar there is sometimes none.

done.title: Training recorded
done.note: At the end, management reviews every item and signs.

5_1.headline: Write down who works for you
5_1.teaser: A list of your suppliers and service providers.
missed: It is not only IT firms that count. It covers every direct supplier and service provider that touches your IT or your data, including for example the tax adviser with access to staff data (§ 30(1) and (2) no. 4 BSIG).
The EU Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) suggests classifying suppliers, for example as critical, strategic and routine.

learn.title: Who works for your company
body: The security of your IT also covers whoever works on it from outside or can reach your data: service providers, software vendors, suppliers. The first step is a list of who they are and what they do for you.
Start with the ones your business could not run without. The list grows over time.
learn.duty: The law requires measures for supply chain security, including in your relationships with your direct suppliers and service providers.

list.title: What your list can look like
list.caption: One line per supplier, with what they do for you:

rows.name: IT provider
rows.detail: looks after servers and accounts, has remote access

rows.name: Microsoft
rows.detail: email and files for all staff

sources.title: Where the names already are
sources.lead: Your company usually knows its suppliers already. Tick where you have looked:

suppliers.title: Your suppliers
suppliers.lead: Whoever you named as the provider of your software and technology is already on it. Enter all the others and say how important each one is to your business. When in doubt, write it down rather than leave it out.

dependence.title: Who could stop you on their own
dependence.lead: How many suppliers are there without whom your business would stop, and for whom no second one is ready?

done.title: Your list is in place
done.note: When a supplier comes along, add it. At the end, management reviews the list.

singlePointOfFailureCount.label: Number of such suppliers
singlePointOfFailureCount.hint: Count the entries where a failure stops your business and there is no replacement.

payables.label: Accounts payable list
payables.text: From accounting. Whoever sends you invoices works for you.

contracts.label: Contracts and subscriptions
contracts.text: Maintenance contracts, software licences, cloud accounts.

provider.label: Your IT provider
provider.text: They know which vendors they use on your behalf.

12_3.headline: Keep the registration up to date
12_3.teaser: When something changes, update it with {authority}.
missed: The directive counts the two weeks from the date of the change (Art. 3(4) NIS 2). Germany counts them from when the company learns of the change (§ 33(5) BSIG). Neither sets a fixed review date.
If your portal also records a contact person, add updating it to what happens when someone leaves the company.
Give a shared mailbox as the point of contact. Then less changes.

learn.title: Keep the details up to date
body: When something changes in what you gave {authority} at registration, update it in its portal.
The law does not require a fixed yearly check. It requires you to be quick when something changes.
learn.duty: Report changes without delay, and at the latest within two weeks.

changes.title: When to update

items.name: Contact person and point of contact
items.detail: someone leaves or takes on a different job

items.name: Name and legal form
items.detail: a change of company name or legal form

items.name: Address, phone and email
items.detail: a move, a new number, a mailbox switched off

items.name: Public IP address ranges
items.detail: a new internet connection or a new provider

items.name: Sector and EU member states
items.detail: a new line of business or services in another country

changes.source: Art. 3(4) NIS 2. In Germany: § 33(1) and (5) BSIG, and the BSI asks for all changes to the registration data to be made in its portal.

contact.title: Who is registered with {authority}
contact.lead: So you know whom {authority} reaches, and notice when that person leaves.

done.title: Contact recorded
done.note: At the end, management reviews every item and signs.

contactPersonName.label: Contact person
contactPersonName.hint: The person entered in the registration portal as the contact person for NIS 2.

contactPersonEmail.label: Contact person's email address
contactPersonEmail.hint: As it appears in the registration portal.

lastRegistrationUpdate.label: Last updated
lastRegistrationUpdate.hint: The day you last changed the details in the portal. Leave it empty if nothing has changed yet.

1_2.headline: Decide who takes care of it
1_2.teaser: Who takes care of information security.
missed: Responsibility stays with management, even when it hands the work to someone else (Art. 20(1) NIS 2).
The law requires no dedicated post for this. Someone can take it on alongside their actual job. Germany's BSI calls the role the information security officer (ISB).

learn.title: Who takes care of it
body: Management carries the responsibility. It approves the measures and oversees their implementation (Art. 20(1) NIS 2). It hands the work to people in the company.
Decide who takes care of it. That can be a single person who does it alongside their job.
learn.duty: Your company has to document that it implements the information security measures.

roles.title: Bring in your team
roles.lead: Invite whoever takes care of it and whoever decides in an incident. Which area each person owns, you set on the team page.

done.title: Roles assigned
done.note: At the end, management reviews every item and signs.

3_1.headline: Plan what happens in an incident
3_1.teaser: Who decides, whom you call, how you reach each other.
missed: The law explicitly names secured voice, video and text communication and, where needed, secured emergency communication systems within the company (§ 30(2) no. 10 BSIG). A phone list on paper does not replace that; it is the fallback when everything else is down.
Decide who writes the report to {authority}. The first report, an early warning, is due at the latest 24 hours after you become aware of a significant incident (Art. 23(4)(a) NIS 2).

learn.title: When something happens
body: During an incident there is no time to work out who does what. So write it down beforehand: who decides, whom you call, and how you reach each other when email and the network are down.
It does not have to be a thick manual. One page that everyone can find is enough to start with.
learn.duty: The law requires your company to be able to handle security incidents.

lead.title: Who leads in an emergency
lead.lead: One person decides what to do. Who helps them, you set in the emergency plan.

escalation.title: Whom you call
escalation.lead: Who gets told when, from IT up to management.

second_way.title: The second way
second_way.caption: How you reach each other when email and the network fail

good.value: An encrypted messenger on the company phones, plus a phone list on paper
good.note: Works even when your own IT is down.

bad.note: If email itself is affected, the message never arrives.

channel.title: Your second way
channel.lead: How you reach each other when your own IT is not working.

plan.title: File the plan
plan.lead: Upload your emergency plan, even if it is only one page. Management approves it.

done.title: Plan recorded
done.note: At the end, management approves the plan with its signature.

incidentLead.label: Incident lead
incidentLead.hint: The person who decides what to do and informs management.

incidentEscalationContacts.label: Escalation contacts
incidentEscalationContacts.hint: Names and phone numbers, by severity of the incident. Include your IT provider's emergency number.

secureCommsChannel.label: Second communication channel
secureCommsChannel.hint: How you reach each other securely when your own IT fails, for example an encrypted messenger on the company phones.

3_3.headline: Know how to report an incident
3_3.teaser: Three reports to {authority}, with fixed deadlines.
missed: The clock runs from when you learn of it, not from when everything is clear. Report early; the second report confirms or updates the first.
In Germany the BSI reads "becoming aware" as the moment someone in the company finds out about the incident during working hours (BSI, Meldepflicht info pack).

If it is a personal data breach, you usually also notify the data protection authority: without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the people affected (Art. 33 GDPR).

learn.title: Reporting an incident
body: If a security incident is significant, you report it to your national CSIRT or {authority}. It is significant if it can seriously disrupt your operations or cause you financial losses, or if it can cause considerable damage to others.
Your country sets the channel. In Germany it is the BSI portal, with the same access as for the registration.
learn.duty: You report significant incidents in three steps with fixed deadlines.

clock.title: The three deadlines
clock.lead: The clock runs from the moment your company learns of the incident. The third deadline starts with the second report.
clock.source: Art. 23(4) NIS 2. If {authority} asks for one, an interim report comes in between. If the incident is still going on after a month, send a progress report instead of the final report, and the final report within a month of dealing with it.

ready.title: What you need for the first report
ready.lead: Settle this now, not in the middle of an emergency:

items.name: Access to the reporting channel
items.detail: in Germany, the BSI portal you have since the registration

items.name: Who reports
items.detail: one person and a deputy, written into the emergency plan

items.name: What you know
items.detail: what is affected, since when, and whether an attack could be behind it

ready.source: Art. 23(1) and (4) NIS 2. In Germany, a company that is not registered yet reports through the BSI's reporting and information portal (BSI, Meldepflicht info pack).

setup.title: Record your reporting setup
setup.lead: One detail: can you report when it matters?

done.title: Reporting prepared
done.note: At the end, management reviews every item and signs.

bsiReportingRegistered.label: Set up to report to {authority}
bsiReportingRegistered.hint: Yes, once you can report through your country's channel. In Germany that is the BSI portal, with the same access as for the registration.

12_2.headline: Register with {authority}
missed: The directive lists your IP ranges among the details you register (Art. 3(4)(b) NIS 2). Your IT provider knows them. Ask them beforehand.
After registering, you report any change to these details within two weeks (Art. 3(4) NIS 2).

learn.title: Registering with {authority}
body: If NIS 2 applies to your company, it registers once with {authority}, the one in charge in your country. You tell it who you are and how to reach you.
Each member state runs its own registration, usually online. The next screen shows where yours is.
learn.duty: Registration is a duty of its own, with a deadline set by your country's law. In Germany it is three months after your company first counts as an important or essential entity.

where.title: Where you register
where.lead: You register in the member state where your company is established. Your country is at the top.
where.source: Art. 26(1) NIS 2: the member state of establishment is in charge. Providers of public electronic communications networks or services register where they provide their services. Providers of cloud computing, data centre and managed services, and similar digital providers, register where their main establishment is.

confirmation.title: Record the registration
confirmation.lead: Two details, so you know later which access was used and on which day.
confirmation.document: Your access to the portal of {authority}

proof.title: File a proof
proof.lead: Keep what the portal shows once the registration is complete: a confirmation, an overview page or an email. A screenshot or a printout records that yours is done.

done.title: Registration recorded
done.note: At the end, management reviews every item and signs.

mukAccountId.label: Account or reference at the portal
mukAccountId.hint: The ID of the account you registered with, or the reference number the portal gave you. In Germany it is the Benutzerkonto-ID of the ELSTER organisation certificate.

bsiRegistrationDate.label: Date of registration
bsiRegistrationDate.hint: The day the registration was submitted in the portal.

2_1.headline: Decide how you rate risks
2_1.teaser: We recommend a ready-made method for this.
missed: Attacks are not the only thing that counts. The law requires an all-hazards approach (§ 30(2) BSIG). The EU directive explicitly requires protecting the physical environment of the systems too (Art. 21(2) NIS 2), for example against fire, water or a power cut.
The method is a start, not a straitjacket. If a level does not fit your company, adjust it. BSI Standard 200-3 explicitly allows for that.

learn.title: How you rate risks
body: Before you write down risks, decide how you rate them. Then everyone in the company rates them by the same rules.

nisd2.eu recommends a simple, ready-made method for this. Every risk gets two ratings: how often can it happen, and how big would the damage be? Together they give one of four levels. The method comes from BSI Standard 200-3, published by Germany's Federal Office for Information Security.
learn.duty: The law requires concepts for risk analysis. It does not prescribe a particular method.

matrix.title: An example risk matrix
matrix.lead: Across: how often something happens. Down: how big the damage would be. Where the two meet is the level.
matrix.source: BSI Standard 200-3, Figure 3. It is given there as an example, to be adapted to the organisation's own needs.

reading.title: How to read the matrix
reading.caption: Six examples, from low to very high. Pick one and the matrix shows where it lands.
examples: A company phone gets lost, which happens once a year to once a month. It is encrypted and can be locked remotely, so the damage is negligible.
A server goes down once a year to once a month. The damage is limited and manageable.
A fire destroys the server room and all data in it. That happens at most every five years, but it would threaten the existence of the company.
Someone falls for a fake email, and invoices with a wrong bank account go out from the hijacked mailbox. That happens once a year to once a month, and the damage is considerable.
Ransomware encrypts every system and the backups too. That happens once every five years to once a year and would threaten the existence of the company.
The unmaintained inventory system goes down several times a month. Each time shipping stops for a day, and the damage is considerable.

adopt.title: Adopt the method
adopt.lead: One click records the method. This is how it will then appear in your records:

lines.label: Method
lines.text: Risk analysis according to BSI Standard 200-3

lines.label: Levels
lines.text: Four for frequency, four for damage, four risk levels

lines.label: Matrix
lines.text: The assignment from Figure 3 of the standard

done.title: Method set
done.note: With the method you rate each risk on its own as you write it down. At the end, management reviews the method and signs.

2_2.headline: Write down what your company has
2_2.teaser: A list of the processes, software and devices you work with.
missed: Software you rent from the cloud belongs on the list too, for example email or accounting.
For processes and applications, the BSI names a responsible person (Standard 200-2). Note who is responsible for each one.

learn.title: What your company works with
body: You can only protect what you know. So write down what your company works with: processes, information, software, devices, data carriers, rooms and networks. Germany's BSI works the same way and calls this step the structure analysis (Standard 200-2).
The list does not have to be perfect. When something new comes along, add it.
learn.duty: The law requires concepts for risk analysis and for managing your IT systems, products and processes. A list of what your company works with is the usual first step for both.

list.title: What your list can look like
list.caption: Short is fine. One line per thing:

sources.title: Where your list already exists
sources.lead: The BSI advises looking for existing overviews. Tick where you have looked:

processes.title: What your company does every day
processes.lead: Tick what runs at your company. When in doubt, write it down rather than leave it out.

business_apps.title: Software for customers, staff and money
business_apps.lead: What you use to serve customers, pay wages and keep the books.

shared_apps.title: Software everyone uses
shared_apps.lead: Email, file storage, chat and anything only your industry has.

technology.title: Technology and rooms
technology.lead: Servers, devices, network and the places where people work.

which_software.title: Which software exactly, and from whom?
which_software.lead: Write down what you actually use, for example "DATEV Unternehmen online" instead of the kind "Accounting". Next to it goes who provides it.

which_technology.title: Which technology exactly, and from whom?
which_technology.lead: The same for devices, network and rooms, for example the name of your internet provider for the internet connection. What you run yourself has no provider.

done.title: Your list is in place
done.note: When something new comes along, add it at any time. Later you rate each entry on its own. At the end, management reviews the list.

ropa.label: Record of processing activities
ropa.text: From data protection (Art. 30 GDPR). It describes what you process personal data for, and often names the software too.

ledger.label: Fixed asset register or inventory list
ledger.text: From accounting. It lists devices and other equipment your company has bought.

provider.label: Your IT provider
provider.text: They know your servers, accounts and cloud services.

2_3.headline: Rate your risks
2_3.teaser: Place every piece of software, every device and every supplier on the matrix.
missed: Suppliers count too. The directive requires supply chain security, including the relationships with each direct supplier or service provider (Art. 21(2)(d) NIS 2), taking into account the vulnerabilities specific to each of them (Art. 21(3) NIS 2).
Rare does not mean small. In the BSI matrix, damage that threatens the existence of the organisation is never low, even if it could occur every 5 years at the most.

learn.title: How big is which risk?
body: Your list is in place: software, technology and suppliers. Now you rate each entry with the method you set. How often does the worst realistic case happen, and how big would the damage be? The matrix turns that into one of four levels.
That shows you where protection is needed first. Individual threats, for example from the BSI's list of elementary threats, can be added afterwards in the risk register.
learn.duty: The law requires policies on risk analysis. How much protection is proportionate depends, among other things, expressly on the likelihood of incidents and their severity (Art. 21(1) NIS 2).

software.title: Rate your software
software.lead: For each one, think of the worst case that is realistic: it goes down, it is attacked or data is lost. How often does something like that happen, and how big would the damage be?

technology.title: Rate your technology and rooms
technology.lead: The same for servers, devices, network and rooms. Think of fire, water and power cuts too.

suppliers.title: Rate your suppliers
suppliers.lead: Here the worst case is that the supplier fails or has a security incident of its own. The level then also shows in your supplier list.

done.title: Your risks are rated
done.note: Low risks are marked "Accept": BSI Standard 200-3 calls it common practice to accept low risks and still monitor them. Everything from "medium" up is marked "Mitigate". You can change either in the risk register. At the end, management reviews the ratings.

2_4.headline: Sign the security policy
2_4.teaser: A short policy that management signs.
missed: Everyone has to know the policy. Announce it to all staff and explain it to new staff before they get access to the systems; Germany's BSI asks for both (IT-Grundschutz ISMS.1.A3, Standard 200-2).

A policy goes out of date. Germany's BSI recommends reviewing it at least every two years (Standard 200-2). Digital providers covered by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 review it at least annually (Annex, point 1.1.2).

learn.title: Your information security policy
body: The information security policy is a short document of principles: what it covers, which objectives your company pursues, who is responsible and how it goes about security. The BSI, Germany's Federal Office for Information Security, calls it the visible commitment of management.

Our template covers what the BSI names as the minimum content. You add what applies to your company, management signs it, and all staff receive it. According to the BSI, more than ten pages are rarely needed.
learn.duty: The law requires policies on information system security (Art. 21(2)(a) NIS 2), and management bodies approve the risk-management measures and oversee their implementation (Art. 20(1) NIS 2). The policy is the document in which management puts that in writing.

leitlinie.title: Your policy
leitlinie.lead: The template covers what the BSI names as the minimum content of a policy, and your company's name is already in it. Add what applies to your company.

document.title: Information security policy of {company}

sections.heading: Scope
sections.text: This policy applies to all of {company}: to all staff, all locations and all information, software, devices and services the company works with. It also applies where a service provider runs any of these for us.

sections.heading: Why information security matters to us
sections.text: Our work depends on information and on the IT that processes it. If they fail, are altered or reach the wrong hands, we cannot deliver our services and we harm our customers. Information security is therefore part of management's responsibilities.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: We protect the availability, confidentiality and integrity of our information and systems. Our services should keep running when something goes wrong, data of customers, staff and partners should be accessible only to those authorised, and our records should stay accurate and complete. These objectives serve the company's aim of delivering reliably and keeping its customers' trust.

sections.heading: Approach
sections.text: We work from the risks. We keep a list of our processes, software, devices and suppliers, assess the risks by a defined method and take measures that fit our size and the risks. In doing so we consider all hazards, including fire, water and power cuts.

sections.heading: Responsibility and organisation
sections.text: Management is responsible for information security. It approves the measures and oversees their implementation. It decides who coordinates information security day to day and provides the time, money and staff for it. All staff follow the rules that derive from this policy and report anything unusual immediately.

sections.heading: Enforcement and review
sections.text: Management enforces this policy and checks regularly whether the measures work. It reviews the policy itself regularly, after major changes in the company and after serious security incidents, and adapts it.

sections.heading: Announcement and entry into force
sections.text: The policy takes effect when management signs it. All staff receive it. New staff get to know it before they are given access to our systems.

clauses.label: Laws and contracts
clauses.heading: Laws and contracts
clauses.text: We comply with the laws and contracts that concern our information security, in particular the national law implementing the NIS 2 Directive, the General Data Protection Regulation and our agreements with customers. All staff are required to observe them.

clauses.label: Contact person
clauses.heading: Contact person
clauses.text: Questions about information security and reports of incidents go to the person who coordinates information security. Who that is can be found in the current overview of roles.

clauses.label: Training
clauses.heading: Training and awareness
clauses.text: All staff receive regular training in information security. Management itself takes part in training regularly.

clauses.label: Suppliers and service providers
clauses.heading: Suppliers and service providers
clauses.text: Anyone who works for us and has access to our systems or data also follows the rules of this policy. We agree this with our suppliers and service providers.

clauses.label: Reporting security incidents
clauses.heading: Reporting security incidents
clauses.text: Staff report security incidents and suspected incidents internally and immediately. The company reports significant incidents to the competent CSIRT or authority within the legal deadlines.

clauses.label: Consequences of violations
clauses.heading: Violations
clauses.text: Violations of this policy and of the rules that derive from it may have consequences under employment law.

clauses.label: Annual review
clauses.heading: Annual review
clauses.text: Management reviews this policy at least once a year.

document.signature: For the management of {company}: place, date, signature

signed.title: Have it signed
signed.lead: Print the policy from the previous step and have management sign it. Then enter the version and the date here.

proof.title: The signed version
proof.lead: Upload a scan or a photo of the signed policy.

done.title: Your policy is in place
done.note: Announce it to all staff, for example by email or on the intranet. When something important changes, update the policy and have it signed again.

policyVersion.label: Version
policyVersion.hint: For example 1.0. Raise it with every change.
